title: Vidura's warning
hookLine: the blind king hears Vidura warn against the game, blames fate, and says yes anyway
carry: karma: calling it fate doesn't undo the choice

cards: A plan needs permission. Duryodhana is a prince, not the king. To invite Yudhishthira to anything, the invitation has to come from his father, Dhritarashtra, the blind king of Hastinapura.
So uncle and nephew go to the palace. Shakuni speaks first, gently, about how pale and thin the prince has grown. And the king, who loves his son, asks him what's wrong.
The plan moves from a road to a throne room, and a father has to decide.

teach.b: Duryodhana tells his father what he told Shakuni, and Shakuni lays out the game. Dhritarashtra hesitates. In the telling, he wants to ask Vidura first, his wise half-brother.

teach.h: VIDURA WARNS: IT WILL END IN QUARREL.
teach.b: Duryodhana pushes back hard: ask Vidura, and Vidura will stop it. He presses until his father gives way. So the king orders a splendid hall built for the game, and only then calls Vidura, not to ask, but to tell him.
Vidura says plainly that he doesn't approve: this game will set the cousins against each other.
And Dhritarashtra answers, in effect: if the gods are kind, no harm will come; what is fated will happen. Then he sends Vidura himself to bring Yudhishthira to play. Now the teaching.
Hindu teaching on karma is not that everything is fixed.
Karma means action, and the fruit that follows it. Some of what reaches us is the ripening of the past, yes. But the choice in front of you is yours, and it makes new karma.

teach.h: CALLING IT FATE DOESN'T UNDO THE CHOICE.
teach.b: Many teachers read Dhritarashtra's line about fate as the moment he hides a choice behind a word. He heard the warning. He loved his son too much to refuse him, and called it destiny.

The epic doesn't let him off; the rest of the poem is the fruit of that yes. For today: when you hear yourself say whatever happens, happens, about something you could still change, that's Dhritarashtra talking.
Karma says the choice is still on your desk.

how: In Hindu retellings, Vidura is remembered as a voice of wise counsel at the Kuru court, the one who tells the blind king what he doesn't want to hear.

o: the blind king who orders a new hall built
the king's wise half-brother, who warns against the game
the uncle who offers to throw the dice for his nephew

games.q: the throne room — tap the pairs.
p: warned the game would bring quarrel

s: he told the king plainly that it would set the cousins against each other.
Dhritarashtra ordered a hall built for the game
a splendid new hall, before he even told Vidura.
in Hindu teaching, karma means everything is already fixed
karma is action and its fruit: some fruit of the past ripens, but each new choice is yours and makes new karma.

games.q: you're Dhritarashtra. Vidura says the game will end in quarrel. your son is desperate. you say 'what is fated will happen.' what does karma say about that?
o: it's out of your hands, so it isn't your karma.
it's still your choice, and its fruit will come to you.
only Vidura's karma is at stake, since he delivers the invitation.
games.why: the king sends Vidura with the invitation and calls it fate. Hindu teaching on karma, and the rest of the epic, say the yes was his, and so was its fruit.

practice: Think of a time you said yes to someone you love when part of you wanted to say no, and picture the moment you gave way. Notice if you told yourself it was out of your hands.

Now say it the karma way, quietly: that was my choice, and I can choose again. No guilt; just ownership. If you pray, you can offer that choice, and that person, in your prayer; if not, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Vidura. The counselor who warns that this game will end in quarrel, and is sent anyway, by a father who called his own choice fate.

orig.note: Sanskrit vidura: the name of Dhritarashtra's half-brother, the counselor who warns against the game.

carryVoice: Your line: karma, calling it fate doesn't undo the choice. Dhritarashtra heard Vidura, and said yes. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Shakuni and Duryodhana persuade Dhritarashtra; the hall built; Vidura's warning; Vidura sent to invite Yudhishthira)
